title: Share entity identity across projections
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The engine can maintain several graph projections simultaneously. Their topology can overlap, and one real-world entity may appear in multiple projections with different context and data.

### Decision

When the same underlying real-world entity is represented in multiple projections, those projections refer to the same underlying entity ID. Each projection may attach its own view and projection-specific data to that entity.

### Consequences

- A test can check that an entity observed in multiple projections refers to the same underlying ID while allowing their projection-specific data to differ.
- Identity resolution needs a defined contract; matching names alone do not prove identity.
- Different groupings and levels of granularity require further design: a group of pods, an individual pod, and a service should not be assumed to share one identity.
- This decision does not prescribe a shared global in-memory graph, storage mechanism, ID format, identity scope, or algorithm.

### Open questions

- How is identity scoped across tenants, sources, clusters and lifetimes?
- Relationship identity is projection-specific; see ADR-003.
- How are aggregate or projection-created entities related to their members?
- How are ambiguous identities, merges, splits, aliases and ID stability on replay handled?

title: Emit complete projection graph diffs
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Each projection produces a graph and change events. Consumers and the verification harness need to understand whether the stream is only a notification or contains sufficient information to reconstruct the graph.

### Decision

Projection change events are complete graph diffs: a consumer can reconstruct the projection graph from the change events, starting from the applicable initial graph and consuming the complete relevant stream.

**Clarification (ADR-021 and ADR-023):** Graph telemetry, such as counts, is separate from graph data and structure. Telemetry has its own stream, separate from graph diffs.

**Correction (ADR-028):** A projection can ignore an input or change so that it causes no change to that projection's graph and produces no graph diff. The earlier interpretation that the graph changed while its diff was suppressed was incorrect. Aggregation is configurable; reconstruction at aggregation boundaries still needs to be specified.

### Consequences

- Verification must compare both checkpoint graphs and the corresponding emitted events.
- Given a defined initial state and stream boundary, applying all changes through a checkpoint should yield the graph at that checkpoint.
- Adds, updates, removals, and any other graph mutation must be representable in the diff stream; exact event types remain to be defined.
- Consumer bootstrap and loss/replay behavior require explicit contracts for a full stream, a starting snapshot, or another agreed baseline.
- This decision does not by itself prescribe a broker, permanent retention, global event ordering, a transport, an event-sourcing implementation, or before-values in every event.

### Open questions

- When one input creates two entities and a relationship, those additions are emitted together in one combined graph diff; see ADR-024. Other atomicity and ordering details remain open.
- How are graph revisions, snapshots and stream positions related?
- Are duplicate delivery, replay, idempotency and retained history required?
- How are projection configuration changes, corrections, merges and expiry encoded?
- Must event IDs, sequence numbers and payloads be byte-identical across deterministic replays, or only semantically equivalent?

title: Give relationships projection-specific identities
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Different projections can represent the same relationship between shared entities. Projections may attach different data to those relationships and may use different relationship granularity.

### Decision

Relationships have projection-specific IDs, even when separate projections represent the same relationship between the same shared entity IDs.

### Consequences

- Entity identity is shared across projections (ADR-001), while relationship identity is scoped to the projection.
- Verification identifies a relationship using its projection context and relationship ID rather than assuming that relationship IDs match across projections.
- Matching endpoints alone must not be assumed to establish relationship equivalence: type, direction, granularity and other properties may matter.
- Whether and how equivalent relationships are associated across projections remains undecided; this decision does not require or rule out such associations.

### Open questions

- What determines a relationship's identity within a projection?
- How are multiple relationships of the same type between the same endpoints distinguished?
- Are relationship IDs stable across replay and projection version changes?
- Relationships are edges and cannot be endpoints of other relationships; see ADR-083, which supersedes ADR-011.

title: Allow independent graph changes to vary in replay order
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The engine aims for deterministic results, but may process independent work in parallel. Complete projection diffs must still reconstruct the correct graph (ADR-002).

### Decision

For the same ordered inputs, rules and time schedule, independent graph changes may be emitted in a different order on replay, provided applying the changes reconstructs the same graph. Exact event ordering is not required for independent changes.

### Consequences

- Conformance checks must not compare all event sequences by strict total order.
- Consumers and tests still need whatever ordering or dependencies are necessary to apply non-independent changes and reconstruct the graph.
- Equivalence must be evaluated at a defined checkpoint with the applicable initial state.
- This decision does not itself specify whether event grouping, event IDs, the exact set of emitted events, or intermediate states must be identical across replays.

### Open questions

- What makes two changes independent, and how is their causal dependency represented?
- What order is guaranteed for changes that affect the same subject or depend on one another?
- Can different runs group the same logical changes into different events?
- How are duplicates, partial deliveries, replay boundaries and graph equality handled?

title: Accept raw input without a required common envelope
body:
**Status:** Accepted as current ingestion behavior  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The engine ingests telemetry in multiple formats and interprets new formats with the help of generated rules. The question asked how telemetry enters the engine today.

### Decision / current behavior

The engine receives source data directly as raw inputs; a common event envelope is not required at the ingestion boundary.

### Consequences

- The verification corpus must include source-native raw inputs without wrapping every record in a mandatory common payload envelope.
- A test runner may still need a separate delivery schedule or sidecar metadata to express ordering and checkpoints; these are harness controls, not assumed fields in the source payload.
- This record does not assert that all data formats, transport types or metadata-free inputs are supported, nor does it preclude optional wrappers or internal normalization.

### Open questions

- Raw inputs include individual events and batches; see ADR-006. File and stream support is not yet specified.
- Which source, tenant, timing and transport metadata is available outside the input payload?
- How are formats identified and how are malformed or unknown inputs handled?
- Where do input event identifiers come from when a raw record has none?

title: Ingest individual events and batches
body:
**Status:** Accepted as current ingestion behavior  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Raw telemetry arrives without a required common envelope (ADR-005). The harness needs to model how records are delivered.

### Decision / current behavior

The engine accepts individual events and batches of records.

### Consequences

- Test schedules should exercise both individual-event and batch ingestion.
- Whether batching affects ordering, atomicity, error handling or output events remains undecided; tests must not assume identical behavior until the contract is agreed.
- This decision does not specify file ingestion, stream protocols, batch size limits or transactional behavior.

### Open questions

- Are batch records ordered, and is that order meaningful?
- Can one invalid record reject the batch or are other records accepted independently?
- Equivalent records delivered individually or in batches must produce the same graph under the conditions in ADR-009; diff grouping is still open.

title: Initialize new projections from existing information
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

A projection may be activated after the engine has already ingested telemetry. Its initial output depends on what information is made available to it.

### Decision

A newly activated projection starts with relevant information already available to the engine, rather than processing only inputs arriving after activation.

### Consequences

- A test must ingest information before activating a projection and check that relevant available information contributes to its initial result.
- Initialization must remain compatible with the complete graph-diff contract in ADR-002; bootstrap mechanics and event boundaries remain to be specified.
- This decision does not guarantee that the engine retains every raw event or all history, nor does it require replaying all historical inputs. It does not define what information is available or relevant.

### Open questions

- Which already-available information is eligible for a newly activated projection, and how is it retained?
- Is initialization derived from current state, retained observations, raw input history, or another source?
- Consumers bootstrap from a snapshot plus subsequent diffs; see ADR-008. How the engine internally builds the initial graph remains open.
- How are inputs arriving during initialization incorporated and ordered?

title: Bootstrap consumers with a snapshot and subsequent diffs
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Consumers need an initial projection graph and must then follow the complete diff stream (ADR-002). A new projection also starts with relevant information already available to the engine (ADR-007).

### Decision

A consumer obtains an initial graph snapshot at a known revision, then applies all subsequent graph changes to stay up to date.

### Consequences

- Snapshot and diff-stream positions must be related clearly enough that a consumer can identify which changes are already reflected in the snapshot and which changes follow it.
- The test harness should reconstruct a later graph from a baseline snapshot and all applicable later diff events, then compare it with an independently obtained checkpoint graph.
- This decision refines ADR-002: the reconstruction baseline is the snapshot; no full stream from an empty graph is required by this decision.
- The snapshot/stream handoff must address concurrent changes, but its mechanism, ordering, retention, delivery guarantees and protocol remain open.

### Open questions

- What identifies a revision and a diff position, and how are they scoped?
- How are gaps and duplicates handled during the snapshot-to-stream handoff?
- Are snapshots atomic or can they be paginated while changes continue?
- How long can a consumer resume from a known revision?

title: Preserve graph semantics across batch boundaries
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The engine accepts individual events and batches (ADR-006). Batch boundaries should have defined effects on output semantics.

### Decision

When the same records are delivered in the same order with the same timing and otherwise equivalent conditions, delivery individually versus in batches must produce the same resulting graph. Batching may affect performance or diff-event grouping.

### Consequences

- Add a metamorphic test comparing graph snapshots after equivalent individually delivered and batched inputs at equivalent processed checkpoints.
- Complete diffs for either run must reconstruct that run's graph from its baseline (ADR-002 and ADR-008); identical diff-event grouping is not required by this decision.
- Real transports may make timing or processing boundaries differ, so tests need an explicit way to define equivalent timing and checkpoints.

### Open questions

- What constitutes equivalent timing and a comparable processing checkpoint?
- Must semantic change sets, intermediate graph states or event grouping also match?
- How are batch errors, partial success, atomicity and within-batch ordering handled?

title: Make late-event handling configurable
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Telemetry can arrive after its valid source event timestamp. Interpreting it according to event time or arrival time may produce different projections.

### Decision

Handling of late data with a valid event timestamp is configurable: the applicable projection or ingestion policy can choose how to handle it.

### Consequences

- Every time-sensitive verification fixture must identify the applicable late-event policy and compare output against that policy.
- Tests should cover relevant supported policies with delayed arrivals and verify graph and diff outcomes.
- Deterministic replay requires pinning the applicable policy along with the input schedule and other relevant configuration.
- The decision does not specify a default policy, lateness thresholds, retention, historical queries, correction event types, or which configuration layer owns the policy.

### Open questions

- Which policies are supported, and where are they configured?
- Can late data revise closed windows or past graph state, and how are corrections represented as complete diffs?
- What happens when event time is missing, malformed or inconsistent with arrival time?
- Are watermarks, explicit clock advancement or another checkpoint mechanism supported?

title: Allow relationships to be endpoints
status: Superseded by ADR-083; this earlier interpretation is incorrect
body:
**Status:** Superseded by ADR-083; this earlier interpretation is incorrect  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Relationships have their own data and projection-specific identities. Some graph concepts need to refer directly to a relationship, such as an incident affecting the connection from Checkout to Payments.

### Decision

Earlier interpretation: a relationship could be the source or target of another relationship. The user corrected this: relationships are edges and cannot point to relationships. See ADR-083. The earlier incident-to-edge example is not a supported edge-to-edge connection under the clarified model.

### Consequences

- Do not use the earlier edge-to-edge endpoint assumption in the conceptual model or verification fixtures.
- Relationships still have their own data and projection-specific identities; those properties do not make an edge an endpoint of another edge.

### Open questions

- See ADR-083 for the corrected endpoint model and remaining questions.

title: Retain the most recent N inputs that affected the graph
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The engine derives graph state from input telemetry. Retaining selected inputs can support inspection of what contributed to graph changes.

### Decision

Each graph element keeps its most recent N inputs that changed that element, subject to the qualification rule in ADR-014: telemetry-only effects do not qualify. The per-element scope is clarified in ADR-077.

### Consequences

- The verification harness needs cases with more than N qualifying inputs and must verify which qualifying inputs remain accessible.
- Inputs that do not affect anything in the graph are not included in this particular retention rule; this does not rule out their storage elsewhere.
- Retained inputs and the complete projection diff stream (ADR-002) are distinct concepts: the decision does not imply they have the same retention period or that N inputs suffice to reconstruct every graph.
- The existence of this bounded retention must not be interpreted as a guarantee of full historical replay, long-term provenance, or complete raw input retention.

### Open questions

- History is per graph element (ADR-077); N is configured per projection (ADR-020). How shared entity IDs interact with history across projections remains open.
- Is N fixed or configurable, and what is its default?
- What precisely qualifies as an input affecting the graph: structural changes, property changes, retained evidence changes, internal state updates or all of these?
- Recency uses the order in which inputs affect the projection; see ADR-016. How concurrent inputs are ordered remains open.
- Is the original raw input retained or a normalized representation, and how are inputs exposed to consumers?
- When one input affects multiple nodes, relationships or projections, how is its retention and attribution tracked?
- Does the buffer survive restarts, and what happens on projection deletion, graph removal, or changes to N?

title: Scope recent graph-affecting inputs per projection
body:
**Status:** Superseded by ADR-077  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

ADR-012 retains the most recent N inputs that affected the graph. Multiple projections can be active simultaneously and can react differently to the same input.

### Decision

Earlier interpretation: each projection keeps a single history of the most recent N inputs affecting its graph. The user corrected this: each graph element has its own history of the most recent N inputs that changed it. See ADR-077.

### Consequences

- Do not test a single projection-wide N-item history as the contract. Verify retention separately for each graph element; the scope of shared entity history across projections remains open.
- An input affecting multiple graph elements can qualify for the history of each element it changed; the physical storage and replay deduplication strategy remain unspecified.
- A shared entity has a separate input history in each projection; see ADR-081.
- This does not decide whether N varies by projection, how recency is ordered, or whether retained inputs survive a restart.

### Open questions

- Which effects qualify an input for a projection's history?
- N is configured per projection; see ADR-020.
- How are ties, late inputs, duplicate deliveries, and batch records counted and ordered?
- Does a configuration change or time-driven update also have associated retained inputs?

title: Exclude unchanged and telemetry-only inputs from retained history
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Each graph element retains its most recent N inputs that changed that element (ADR-077). As clarified by the user, a count is graph telemetry, separate from graph data and structure; a repeated input can increment telemetry without changing the graph.

### Decision

An input that matches a projection but leaves its graph data and structure unchanged is not added to any element's recent graph-affecting input history, including when it increases a telemetry count. An input that changes some elements qualifies for those affected elements, subject to the precise effect rules still being defined.

### Consequences

- Retained input history is not a complete log of all matched inputs or telemetry updates; telemetry can change without the input entering that history.
- Complete graph diffs (ADR-002) apply to graph changes. Telemetry has a separate stream (ADR-023).
- Tests should include a repeated input that changes telemetry without changing the graph, then check history retention, graph diffs and telemetry independently.
- An input that increases a count and changes a relationship from healthy to degraded qualifies for retention; see ADR-015. Other mixed effects remain to be specified.

### Open questions

- Which graph data or structural changes qualify an input for retention?
- Which measurements are graph telemetry and which values are graph data?
- Is this rule fixed for all projections or configurable?
- How is an input that affects several entities or projections classified and attributed?

title: Retain an input when it also causes a status change
status: Accepted; health-status classification clarified by ADR-022
body:
**Status:** Accepted; health-status classification clarified by ADR-022  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Telemetry-only effects do not qualify an input for recent-input history (ADR-014), but an input can have several effects. The user clarified that relationship health status is graph data (ADR-022), while a count is graph telemetry (ADR-021).

### Decision

An input that increments a telemetry count and also changes a relationship's graph health status from healthy to degraded is retained in that relationship's recent-input history. The graph status change qualifies the input; the telemetry count alone would not.

### Consequences

- A telemetry count update does not disqualify an input that also makes a qualifying graph status change.
- A test should contrast a count-only input with one that increments a count and triggers a healthy-to-degraded relationship change, checking both graph diffs and recent-input history.
- This decision establishes the specified status transition as qualifying; it does not define every qualifying transition or other graph change.

### Open questions

- Do all status changes qualify, including recovery, unknown and stale transitions?
- Which attribute, structural, evidence and relationship changes qualify?
- How are effects attributed when one input and other concurrent inputs jointly cause a transition?

title: Order retained inputs by projection processing order
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Each graph element keeps its most recent N qualifying inputs (ADR-077), with N configured per projection (ADR-020). Event timestamps and arrival order can differ from the order in which inputs affect a projection.

### Decision

Determine recency by the order in which inputs affect the projection. A late input with an old source timestamp may therefore be among the most recently retained inputs.

### Consequences

- Retention tests must exercise late inputs and verify processing-order recency rather than sorting solely by source event time.
- Configurable late-event interpretation (ADR-010) is distinct from retention ordering: the chosen late-event policy determines effects, while this decision determines recency among qualifying inputs.
- When parallel processing allows independent changes to appear in varying order (ADR-004), the order and replay equivalence of bounded retained histories require an explicit contract.

### Open questions

- Inputs are not processed in parallel within a projection; see ADR-017. Input scheduling and replay order remain open.
- Must the retained set or order be identical across deterministic replays when independent changes can be processed in different orders?
- Is the order observable to consumers, and how are ties represented?
- What happens when an input affects a projection more than once, including through correction or reprocessing?

title: Process inputs sequentially within each projection
body:
**Status:** Accepted as stated engine behavior  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Each projection retains qualifying inputs by processing order (ADR-016). We asked how concurrent processing within a projection affects reproducibility.

### Decision / current behavior

There is no parallelism within a projection: inputs are processed sequentially within that projection.

### Consequences

- The previous question about simultaneous application within one projection does not apply under this behavior.
- The order in which inputs are selected or delivered to the projection still needs to be defined; sequential processing alone does not guarantee identical ordering across runs.
- The relationship between independently emitted diffs, batching and replay determinism (ADR-004 and ADR-009) remains to be clarified.
- This decision does not specify whether separate projections process concurrently, nor does it prescribe threads, actors, locks or other implementation mechanisms.

### Open questions

- Each projection processes accepted inputs in ingestion order; see ADR-018. How that order is assigned across sources remains open.
- How are batches, late events, timers, configuration changes and replay interleaved?
- Can separate projections process simultaneously and progress at different rates?

title: Process projection inputs in ingestion order
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Inputs are processed sequentially within a projection (ADR-017), and recent qualifying inputs are ordered by their effects on that projection (ADR-016). Source event time can differ from ingestion time.

### Decision

Each projection processes its accepted inputs in ingestion order, including late-arriving inputs. Configurable late-event handling (ADR-010) determines how a late event is interpreted; it does not require reordering accepted inputs by source time.

### Consequences

- The verification harness must preserve and express the accepted ingestion order separately from source event timestamps.
- Replay tests should provide the same accepted input order, policy, time controls and other relevant conditions when comparing deterministic results.
- Input history follows the actual order in which qualifying inputs affect the projection; ingestion order alone does not define effects caused later by timers, corrections or reprocessing.
- Sequential ingestion order does not automatically define order among multiple diffs produced by one input; ADR-004 permits independent output changes to vary in order.

### Open questions

- What defines acceptance and ingestion order across multiple sources, batches and retries?
- How is that order exposed for checkpoints and deterministic replay?
- How are timer events, projection configuration changes, corrections and reprocessing interleaved with input processing?
- How do duplicate and rejected inputs participate in ordering?

title: Process repeated input deliveries separately
body:
**Status:** Superseded by ADR-021  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Raw inputs may be delivered more than once. Identical records can also represent distinct observations, so content equality alone does not establish whether a delivery should be ignored.

### Decision

Earlier interpretation of the user's answer: repeated deliveries were treated as completely independent graph observations. The user clarified that repeated input can affect graph telemetry while producing no change to graph data or structure. See ADR-021; do not treat the earlier interpretation as the current contract.

### Consequences

- The earlier recommendation to count repeated deliveries independently must not be used as an unconditional expected result until ADR-021 is clarified.
- A repeated delivery can update telemetry without changing the graph and is then excluded from retained recent-input history under ADR-014.
- Identical content must not be assumed to imply a unique event. The existing decision does not specify behavior of external transports, rejection or other source-specific preprocessing before acceptance.
- Deterministic replay must reproduce the delivery sequence, including repetitions, for equivalent outputs.

### Open questions

- Can a source-specific rule explicitly implement idempotency, or is processing every delivery mandatory at all layers?
- How does the engine distinguish separately delivered records in provenance if the raw input has no unique ID?
- What are the delivery guarantees for projection diff consumers, and are they independent of input delivery semantics?

title: Configure retained-input limit per projection
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Each graph element retains its most recent N qualifying inputs (ADR-077), and different projections may have different history needs.

### Decision

Each projection can choose its own limit N for retained qualifying inputs.

### Consequences

- Tests should configure different limits for simultaneously active projections and check retention independently.
- The configured limit applies to per-element histories (ADR-077); physical input storage may be shared or deduplicated internally without changing observable behavior. Cross-projection scoping of shared entities remains open.
- Retention testing must account for inputs excluded because they are unchanged or count-only (ADR-014), and for qualifying combined effects (ADR-015).

### Open questions

- What are the default, minimum and maximum limits? Can N be zero or unlimited?
- What happens when N changes while the projection is active?
- Is this configuration part of the projection configuration graph and version?
- Does the retained history persist across restarts or projection reactivation?

title: Distinguish implicit graph deduplication from telemetry
body:
**Status:** Accepted; matching semantics open  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The user clarified: “count is graph telemetry, not part of the graph data or structure. Same input won’t change the graph, but of course affect telemetry. That’s the implicit deduplication.” The earlier ADR-019 interpretation incorrectly conflated the graph with telemetry about the graph.

### Decision / current behavior

The same input does not change the graph when delivered again, but it can affect graph telemetry, such as a count. This is the engine's implicit deduplication. Graph telemetry is separate from graph data and structure. The exact criteria for recognizing the same input remain to be defined.

### Consequences

- ADR-019's unconditional interpretation of how repeated input affects the graph is superseded.
- The harness must deliver the same input twice and check that the repeated delivery leaves graph data and structure unchanged while verifying the specified telemetry effect independently.
- A telemetry count may increase without constituting a graph change. Under ADR-014 a telemetry-only effect does not qualify the input for recent graph-affecting input history.
- A complete graph diff stream must reflect actual graph changes. Telemetry has a separate stream (ADR-023).
- Deduplication of input deliveries, interpreted observations, graph elements, output diffs and retained-input history are distinct possibilities and must not be conflated.

### Open questions

- Is implicit deduplication simply the no-op effect of applying an already-represented graph change, or does it use an explicit input identity, cache or other mechanism?
- What makes two inputs effectively the same for graph purposes: content, source identity, event ID, transformed graph operations, or something else?
- Which counts or other telemetry change on a repeated observation, and how are telemetry changes exposed?
- How does deduplication interact with count-only history exclusion, projections, replay and different input formats?

title: Treat relationship health status as graph data
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Graph telemetry such as counts is separate from graph data and structure (ADR-021). The classification of relationship health status affects whether a status transition changes the graph, appears in graph diffs, and qualifies an input for recent-input history.

### Decision

A relationship's health status, such as healthy or degraded, belongs to graph data.

### Consequences

- Changing a relationship's health status changes graph data and must be represented in the complete graph-diff stream (ADR-002).
- A healthy-to-degraded change caused by an input qualifies that input for the projection's recent-input history, even if the same input also updates a telemetry count (ADR-015).
- An unchanged relationship status and otherwise unchanged graph, accompanied only by a telemetry update, does not qualify the input for that history (ADR-014).
- This decision does not classify all possible measurements, entity attributes, health signals, or derived information as graph data; those distinctions remain open.

### Open questions

- Is an entity's health status also graph data?
- What status vocabulary and transition semantics are supported, and can projections define their own?
- What evidence and policy are associated with a status change?
- Are relationship and entity health states intrinsic graph properties or entities/relationships in their own right?

title: Use a separate telemetry stream
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Counts and other graph telemetry are separate from graph data and structure (ADR-021), while graph changes are emitted as complete diffs (ADR-002). The user corrected an initial choice of query-only output to specify a separate stream.

### Decision

Telemetry is available through a stream separate from the graph-diff stream.

### Consequences

- The harness must verify graph snapshots, graph diff events and telemetry stream outputs as distinct observable results.
- A repeated input can leave graph data and structure unchanged while affecting telemetry, which is observed through the separate stream.
- If a telemetry update coincides with a graph-data change, such as a health-status transition, the graph change is still represented in the graph-diff stream.
- This decision does not specify telemetry event granularity, delivery guarantees, retention, sampling, aggregation, ordering across streams, or whether telemetry can also be queried.

### Open questions

- Does the telemetry stream publish each observation, a running count, periodic aggregates, or configurable combinations?
- How are telemetry items associated with projections, entities and relationships?
- Can a test align graph-diff and telemetry outputs with one input or checkpoint?
- Can consumers also query current or historical telemetry?

title: Combine related graph additions from one input in a diff
status: Conditional on projection setup; see ADR-025
body:
**Status:** Conditional on projection setup; see ADR-025  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

One input can produce several graph changes. The user was asked how a single input that creates two entities and a relationship should appear in the graph-diff stream.

### Decision

For that case, the user initially selected one combined graph-diff event containing the two entity additions and relationship addition. The user clarified that behavior depends on projection setup, which can ignore inputs or aggregate changes. Treat the single combined event as an expected result only for a projection configured to produce it, not as a universal rule.

### Consequences

- The harness should include a fixture where one input causes those three changes, and expect one diff event only when the selected projection setup specifies that behavior.
- Applying the combined event must result in a graph containing both entities and the relationship, in accordance with the complete-diff contract (ADR-002).
- The question of whether every graph change caused by any one input must always be grouped into one event remains open; this answer establishes the behavior for the described case.
- Atomic visibility, error handling, representation of updates and removals, and effects distributed over time remain unspecified.

### Open questions

- Which projection setups emit one combined event, and which ignore inputs or aggregate changes?
- Is the combined event applied atomically by consumers, including error and partial-delivery behavior?
- Can one input trigger later graph changes due to timers or other inputs, and how are those grouped?
- How are no-op inputs and multiple inputs in a batch represented in diff events?

title: Configure projection diff behavior and allow stacked projections
body:
**Status:** Accepted principle; detailed semantics open  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The earlier discussion assumed a universal correspondence between one input and one combined graph-diff event. The user clarified that diff behavior depends on projection setup, diffs can be muted or aggregated, projections can stack on each other, and the projection language is like math.

### Decision

Projection setup determines which incoming information affects the projection and how resulting changes are aggregated. An ignored input/change does not change that projection's graph and yields no diff (ADR-028). Projections can be stacked on top of other projections. The projection language is mathematical in character; its precise syntax and semantics remain open.

### Consequences

- Test fixtures must define projection configuration, stacking, and output behavior before specifying expected graph diffs.
- One input need not universally produce one emitted diff; a configured projection may ignore information or aggregate changes. ADR-024 is conditional, not a general event-grouping guarantee.
- Multi-projection tests must cover an upstream projection feeding a downstream projection, including how graph changes propagate according to configuration.
- The interaction between aggregation and the complete-diff/snapshot reconstruction decisions (ADR-002 and ADR-008) requires clarification.
- Stacking does not by itself establish that all projection dependencies are acyclic, or that downstream projections consume exactly the same public stream as external consumers.

### Open questions

- What conditions cause an input or upstream change to be ignored by a projection?
- What does aggregation preserve, what triggers emission, and can a consumer reconstruct intermediate graph states?
- What does a downstream projection consume: upstream graph, diffs, raw input, or an internal representation?
- Are projection stacks allowed to contain cycles, and what is the mathematical semantics of evaluation?
- What are the language's fundamental operators, values, composition rules, and determinism guarantees?

title: Omit muted changes from the diff stream
status: Superseded by ADR-028; earlier interpretation was incorrect
body:
**Status:** Superseded by ADR-028; earlier interpretation was incorrect  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Projection configurations may mute or aggregate diffs (ADR-025). The earlier complete-diff decision (ADR-002) needs a precise boundary when muting is enabled.

### Decision

Earlier interpretation: the graph changes but the change is omitted from the diff stream. The user corrected this: the projection fully ignores the input/change, so there is no change to its graph and consequently no graph diff. See ADR-028.

### Consequences

- Do not use the earlier assumption that the projection graph changes silently. Correct tests assert that the projection graph remains unchanged and no diff is produced for the ignored input/change.
- The earlier conclusion that an omitted diff necessarily prevents reconstruction does not apply to a change that never occurred in the projection graph.

### Open questions

- How do ignoring and aggregation interact in a projection configuration?

title: Muted upstream changes do not trigger downstream projections
body:
**Status:** Clarified by ADR-028  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Projections may be stacked (ADR-025). The user corrected the premise: a change ignored by a projection does not change that projection's graph or produce a diff (ADR-028).

### Decision

A projection stacked downstream does not react through the upstream diff path when the upstream projection ignores an input/change and produces no diff for it. The user answered “No” to the earlier question, but the incorrect premise about a silent upstream graph change is withdrawn.

### Consequences

- A fixture should configure projection A to ignore an input/change, assert A's graph is unchanged and no diff is emitted, and assert B receives no corresponding diff through that upstream path.
- A separate fixture should verify B's behavior when A emits the corresponding change.
- B can differ from A for other configured reasons, but a silent mutation of A must not be inferred from an ignored input/change.
- This decision does not resolve how B initializes from existing information (ADR-007), whether B has other inputs, or what happens when A aggregates or later emits other changes.

### Open questions

- How does a newly activated B initialize from A's available graph and earlier emitted information?
- Can B also consume raw input or other upstream projections?
- What does B receive when A aggregates changes, and can aggregated output include effects of earlier muted changes?
- What are the ordering, revision and checkpoint semantics across a projection stack?

title: Ignored projection input causes no graph change or diff
body:
**Status:** Accepted correction  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The user clarified: “It’s not muted, its fully ignored. No diff comes out, because the projection will not lead to a change in graph.” The earlier ADR-026 incorrectly assumed that the graph changed while the diff was suppressed.

### Decision

When a projection ignores an input or upstream change, that ignored input/change does not change that projection's graph, so it produces no corresponding graph diff.

### Consequences

- A test for ignored inputs checks graph unchanged and no corresponding graph diff, rather than expecting a silent graph mutation.
- A downstream projection receives no corresponding diff through that upstream path when no diff is produced.
- This corrects ADR-026 and the affected reasoning in ADR-002, ADR-025 and ADR-027; it does not establish that projection aggregation is lossless or specify aggregation boundaries.
- The exact projection language constructs and the relationship between initialization, filtering, and downstream input remain open.

### Open questions

- What conditions make a projection ignore an input or upstream change?
- Can a downstream projection have other sources that react independently to the same original input?
- What does aggregation emit and when, and what graph snapshots are available between aggregation boundaries?
- How do new stacked projections initialize from available upstream information?

title: Support graph grouping and aggregation over time
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Projection behavior is configurable and projections can be stacked (ADR-025). Aggregation may describe both a graph's representation and how changes are combined over time.

### Decision

Projections support both combining multiple entities or relationships into a higher-level graph representation and combining multiple incoming changes over time before producing a resulting graph change.

### Consequences

- Verification fixtures must test graph grouping and time-based change aggregation separately and in combination where configured.
- Grouped entities need a clear identity and membership contract in light of shared entity identity (ADR-001); no particular group ID scheme is decided.
- Time-based aggregation requires explicit test schedules, evaluation boundaries and expected graph/diff checkpoints. No particular windowing, trigger or clock behavior is assumed.
- When projections are stacked, tests must verify how an aggregated upstream result affects a downstream projection under the selected configuration.
- This decision does not determine whether intermediate inputs or changes are visible in snapshots, whether aggregation is lossless, or whether intermediate state can be reconstructed.

### Open questions

- What mathematical operators define grouping and aggregation?
- How are member identities, group identity, provenance and removal represented?
- What determines when an aggregation emits or updates the resulting graph?
- What happens when late inputs or configuration changes affect an aggregation?

title: Allow graph and graph diffs as projection inputs
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Projections are composable and can be stacked (ADR-025). The user clarified that a projection can take a graph and graph diffs as inputs, as well as other inputs.

### Decision

A projection can receive a graph and graph diffs as inputs, in addition to other kinds of inputs. These inputs enable graph-oriented composition and do not replace other supported input types.

### Consequences

- The conceptual harness must support test cases with input graphs, graph-diff inputs, other input formats, and combinations of these.
- Stacked-projection tests must specify each projection's inputs and expected output graph and diffs; a projection can consume more than one kind of input.
- A test should cover an input graph followed by graph diffs, and verify downstream output at specified checkpoints. It should also cover a projection using graph inputs alongside other input types when supported by its configuration.
- This decision does not determine whether the graph and diffs always form a snapshot-plus-revision pair, how they are synchronized, or which other inputs can be combined in a single projection.

### Open questions

- A projection can receive multiple input graphs at the same time; see ADR-031. Multiple diff streams and their coordination need clarification.
- A graph and its diff input are related as a starting state and subsequent changes to the same graph; see ADR-042.
- How are input identities, timestamps, ordering and checkpoints coordinated across mixed input types?
- Which non-graph inputs can a projection consume directly, and are they raw or interpreted first?
- How are invalid diffs, unavailable input graphs, and cycles between projections handled?

title: Allow multiple graph inputs to one projection
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

A projection can accept graph and diff inputs alongside other input types (ADR-030). The user was asked whether it can accept more than one graph at the same time.

### Decision

One projection can take multiple input graphs simultaneously.

### Consequences

- Verification fixtures should include multiple input graphs with both overlapping and distinct entities, and assert the configured output graph and diffs.
- Shared underlying entity identity (ADR-001) and projection-specific relationship identity (ADR-003) need to be respected when fixtures describe inputs and expected outputs.
- This decision does not specify a fixed set of graph operators, automatic merging, conflict resolution, scheduling, or the number of diff streams supported.

### Open questions

- Which graph operations does the projection language support?
- The projection decides how to handle conflicting property values; see ADR-032.
- How does the projection order, synchronize and checkpoint changes from multiple input graphs?
- Can each input graph have an associated independent diff stream?

title: Let the projection resolve conflicting input values
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

A projection can consume multiple graphs simultaneously (ADR-031), and the same underlying entity can appear in more than one projection (ADR-001). Different input graphs can contain different values for the same entity property.

### Decision

The projection decides how conflicting values are resolved. Its configuration defines whether to choose, combine, preserve, or otherwise handle the values.

### Consequences

- Each conflict fixture must specify the projection configuration and expected result; the harness must not assume a universal source precedence or automatic merge.
- Test cases should exercise at least the resolution modes the projection language actually supports, including reproducibility for equivalent ordered inputs.
- If the projection preserves several values or produces an unresolved conflict, its graph representation and diff semantics must be defined by the applicable configuration.
- This decision does not prescribe the available operators, a default resolution when the configuration is silent, or a provenance schema.

### Open questions

- Which conflict-resolution operators and defaults exist?
- Can the projection preserve multiple values, their sources, and their temporal applicability?
- How are configuration changes and late updates to one input graph reflected in the output?

title: Correlate using supplied evidence and inference rules
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The test corpus should exercise network and HTTP records together. Network records can contain IP addresses while HTTP inputs can use service names, so correlating them can require additional evidence or inference.

### Decision

The engine can correlate inputs using both supplied mapping evidence and inference rules, depending on what evidence is available.

### Consequences

- Verification fixtures should include cases with explicit IP-to-service evidence, cases using applicable inference rules, and cases with insufficient evidence.
- Expected correlation and entity identities must follow the selected evidence and rule configuration; a match should not be assumed merely from similar-looking inputs.
- Deterministic replay should pin relevant rules, inputs and ordering. The availability of inference does not by itself determine whether inference is probabilistic, AI-generated, or deterministic.
- This decision does not define a confidence model, rule precedence, behavior for ambiguous matches, or whether a specific inference is accepted.

### Open questions

- Which evidence and inference rules exist today, and how are they configured and versioned?
- What happens when evidence is missing, ambiguous or conflicting?
- Can inferred matches be revised, and how does revision affect identities, graph diffs and retained inputs?
- Is correlation evaluated globally, within a tenant, per projection, or at other scopes?

title: Let projections decide how to represent uncertain matches
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Network and HTTP inputs may contain incomplete evidence that an address and a service refer to the same underlying entity. Projections can use evidence and inference rules (ADR-033).

### Decision

The projection's rules decide how to represent an uncertain match. The engine does not impose one universal representation for all projections in this case.

### Consequences

- Test fixtures must state the relevant projection policy and compare the resulting graph and diffs against that policy.
- Different projections can legitimately represent uncertainty differently while adhering to the shared underlying entity identity contract where an identity is established (ADR-001).
- Examples such as separate entities or a tentative relationship are possibilities for a policy; this decision does not establish which representations the language currently supports.
- Exact criteria for uncertainty, identity assignment, confidence and later revisions remain open.

### Open questions

- What uncertainty representations and inference policies are supported?
- How does a projection revise its output when better evidence arrives?
- Can different projections make conflicting identity claims, and how does that interact with shared entity identity?
- What identifies the same candidate across multiple input sources?

title: Let tests choose exact or partial graph expectations
body:
**Status:** Accepted for verification harness  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

A small scenario may specify an entire expected graph, while a larger scenario may focus on selected entities, relationships or graph properties. The user stated that the comparison depends on the test and confirmed that each test can choose.

### Decision

The verification harness supports both exact graph comparison and targeted assertions about selected graph facts. Each test declares whether its graph expectation is complete or partial.

### Consequences

- In exact mode, comparison should detect missing, unexpected and differing graph elements within the explicitly defined comparison scope.
- In partial mode, passing assertions establish only the declared properties; unasserted portions of the graph have not been verified.
- Each test still needs explicit comparison rules for identity, property values, scope, ordering, and permitted normalization or tolerance.
- This decision covers graph expectations, not the independent completeness or comparison modes for emitted diffs or the retained-input history.

### Open questions

- What formats should represent complete snapshots and partial assertions?
- How are graph equivalence, volatile fields, aggregation and projection-specific identity expressed?
- Should diff streams and retained inputs have their own exact-versus-partial comparison modes?

title: Provide machine-readable tests and graphical views
body:
**Status:** Accepted for verification harness  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The harness must describe test scenarios and expected graphs so they can be executed and reviewed. The engine's graph export format has not yet been defined.

### Decision

Use a machine-readable test format and provide a graphical view for inspecting and editing test cases and expected graphs. Tests can also be edited through their files.

### Consequences

- Test scenarios and expected outputs must be representable as structured data that a runner can consume.
- The design must support visual inspection and editing of test scenarios and expected graphs; details of editing operations, integration and visualization are not decided.
- The machine-readable test representation need not match the engine's eventual runtime graph export format.
- This decision does not choose JSON, YAML, a graph serialization, a UI technology, or how concurrent file and visual edits are reconciled.

### Open questions

- Portable test files are authoritative; see ADR-037.
- What test details beyond graph topology should be visualized: time, diffs, assertions, projections and input traces?
- How are large graphs, exact versus partial expectations, and failure explanations displayed?

title: Use portable test files as the authoritative representation
body:
**Status:** Accepted for verification harness  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Tests can be inspected and edited visually as well as through machine-readable files (ADR-036). They also need to be shareable and runnable by automated systems.

### Decision

Tests are saved as portable files that can be committed to Git and run in CI. The visual editor reads and writes the same test files used by automated runs.

### Consequences

- Test data, projection configurations, schedules, expected graph assertions and diff expectations need portable file representations or explicit references to such files.
- A test should be runnable without requiring the visual editor, assuming its runtime dependencies and referenced inputs are available.
- Visual editing must preserve the meaning of the test as executed by the runner; round-trip verification should be included when the editor exists.
- This decision does not select a serialization format, repository structure, UI technology, storage path, or strategy for concurrent edits.

### Open questions

- Human-edited test descriptions use YAML (ADR-038). Formats for raw inputs, projection definitions, snapshots and diff expectations still need clarification.
- How are large datasets stored or referenced without undermining portability and reproducibility?
- How are test-file schema versions and migration handled?
- Which test artifacts are generated, hand-authored, or editable in the UI?

title: Use YAML for human-edited test descriptions
body:
**Status:** Accepted for verification harness  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Tests are portable files that can be edited directly or through a visual editor, committed to Git, and run in CI (ADR-036 and ADR-037).

### Decision

Use YAML for the human-edited test descriptions.

### Consequences

- The harness and visual editor need a well-defined YAML test-description schema and consistent validation.
- Test descriptions must remain portable and suitable for version control and automated execution.
- This choice does not require rewriting original input records into YAML; the corpus can preserve source-native formats.
- This decision does not yet select formats for graph snapshots, diff expectations, projection definitions, large datasets, or the engine's runtime API.

### Open questions

- Expected graphs and diff assertions are inline in each YAML test description; see ADR-039.
- How are schema versions, unambiguous scalar types, references and validation errors handled?
- How should large or source-native input fixtures be referenced from a description?

title: Keep graph and diff expectations inline in test YAML
body:
**Status:** Accepted for verification harness  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Human-edited test descriptions use YAML (ADR-038). A test must describe expected graphs and diff events at defined checkpoints.

### Decision

Keep each test and its expected graph and diff results together inline in one YAML test description.

### Consequences

- A reviewer can read the scenario and its expected results together.
- The schema and visual editor must support inline complete or partial graph assertions (ADR-035) and inline diff expectations.
- Large expected graphs or long diff streams may make test files substantial; the design must consider usability without assuming an external expectation-file mechanism.
- This decision concerns expected graphs and diffs. Original source-native input collections live in separate files (ADR-040).

### Open questions

- How are checkpoints, graph identities, diff order constraints, and exact-versus-partial matching represented inline?
- Can generated or templated fixtures expand into the inline test description, and how are those expansions reviewed?
- How are source-native inputs supplied while keeping tests portable?

title: Keep source-native input datasets in separate files
body:
**Status:** Accepted for verification harness  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Expected graph and diff assertions are inline in YAML test descriptions (ADR-039), while the corpus can contain large collections of records in their original source formats.

### Decision

Keep source-native input datasets in separate files and reference them from the YAML test description.

### Consequences

- Raw input formats need not be rewritten as YAML merely to use them in a test.
- Tests need portable references to their input files, consistent with version-controlled test files (ADR-037).
- Input scheduling, batching, source metadata and checkpoint controls still require explicit representation in the test description or another defined harness mechanism.
- This decision does not specify a path scheme, large-file storage mechanism, compression, external data access or dataset versioning.

### Open questions

- How are input files resolved and their contents verified in local and CI environments?
- How are large datasets versioned or generated reproducibly?
- How are interleaving and ingestion order expressed when a scenario reads multiple files?

title: Allow a projection to verify another projection's output
body:
**Status:** Accepted capability; verification semantics open  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Projections can accept graphs, graph diffs and other inputs (ADR-030), can consume multiple graphs (ADR-031), and can be stacked (ADR-025). The user pointed out that a projection can therefore verify another projection's output.

### Decision

A projection can be used to verify the output of another projection. A verification harness may use this composability as part of its evaluation design.

### Consequences

- Explore verification projections that consume actual projection output and independently specified expected graph or diff information and produce a comparison result, subject to supported language operations.
- The test oracle must not be assumed independent merely because the comparison is implemented as another projection: expected results and verification semantics need separate validation.
- Include small independently specified scenarios and deliberate defects to test the verification projection; avoid relying solely on the engine under test to manufacture both actual and expected answers.
- This capability does not yet mandate that every test use a verification projection, define how assertions or failures are represented, or establish which comparison operators already exist.

### Open questions

- Should the verification projection itself run in the same engine instance, a separate instance, or either?
- How should expected graphs, diff sequences, comparison rules and checkpoint boundaries be supplied to it?
- Does the verification projection produce a graph of mismatches, a pass/fail result, diffs, or a combination?
- How is the verification projection validated independently and kept isolated from the behavior being tested?

title: Pair graph inputs with diffs for that graph
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

A projection can receive graph and graph-diff inputs alongside other inputs (ADR-030). The relationship between an input graph and its diff stream needs to be explicit.

### Decision

When a projection receives a graph and graph diffs as a pair, the graph provides a starting state and the diffs describe subsequent changes to that same graph.

### Consequences

- Test fixtures should establish an initial graph and then feed diffs against that graph in the specified sequence, asserting the projection's output at checkpoints.
- Graph and diff inputs must be associated clearly enough that a diff is applied to the intended graph, particularly when a projection takes multiple graph inputs (ADR-031).
- The test must verify the handoff between initial state and subsequent changes, including behavior for gaps or invalid diffs once that behavior is defined.
- This decision does not specify the transport, revision encoding, delivery guarantees or cross-input ordering.

### Open questions

- Can a projection receive graph-diff input without first receiving an initial graph, such as an explicitly empty starting graph?
- How are graph revisions, diff positions, gaps and duplicates represented?
- How are updates from several input graph/diff pairs interleaved and checkpointed?
- How does the projection handle invalid or out-of-order diffs?

title: Allow a base projection to handle input interpretation
status: Accepted capability; rule placement remains flexible
body:
**Status:** Accepted capability; rule placement remains flexible  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

AI can create rules for a new input format, and projections can be layered. When asked whether such rules are shared or per projection, the user explained that a base projection might handle the input.

### Decision

A base projection can handle input interpretation and feed its output to layered projections. The model should support this composition without imposing a single mandatory, global preprocessing layer.

### Consequences

- Verification scenarios should cover a base projection interpreting input followed by one or more downstream projections.
- Tests must specify the actual projection graph, input rule and version, and expected outputs at each relevant projection.
- This decision does not establish that all input formats must pass through a base projection, that all generated rules are globally shared, or whether downstream projections can add or replace interpretation rules.
- Rule generation and execution boundaries, and deterministic replay of generated rules, remain to be specified.

### Open questions

- Are generated rules themselves represented as projection configuration graphs?
- Can distinct base projections interpret the same source differently?
- Can downstream projections add or replace format-specific interpretation?
- How are accepted generated rules versioned and selected for replay?

title: Test AI rule generation and fixed-rule graph behavior
body:
**Status:** Accepted for verification harness  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

AI can create a rule for a new input format, while graph transformations need a deterministic verification contract. A base projection may perform input interpretation (ADR-043).

### Decision

The harness tests both AI rule generation and graph behavior using a fixed generated rule. Rule-generation evaluation and fixed-rule graph verification are distinct parts of the overall test design.

### Consequences

- Rule-generation tests need representative unseen formats and independently specified criteria for evaluating generated rules.
- Fixed-rule tests must identify the actual rule used so graph and diff behavior can be reproduced under equivalent inputs, projection definitions and time controls.
- The test plan must not assume that separate AI generation runs always produce the same rule merely because their examples are the same.
- This decision does not exclude an end-to-end test that generates a rule and immediately processes data with it; how such a test evaluates variable generation outcomes remains open.

### Open questions

- What is the generated rule's representation, identity and versioning scheme?
- Which portions of rule generation are evaluated automatically or reviewed manually?
- How are generation examples separated from held-out verification examples?
- How are model, prompt and external context captured when reproducibility is needed?

title: Apply projection configuration changes to future inputs
body:
**Status:** Superseded by ADR-064  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

A projection has a configuration and an output graph. The user clarified that inputs may change the projection's graph, while a change to the projection itself has no immediate effect on that output graph; later inputs might.

### Decision

Earlier interpretation: changing a projection's configuration does not by itself change its existing output graph. The user corrected this: any projection edit outputs a new graph, which can be the same as the prior graph; if it is the same there is no diff. See ADR-064.

**Scaffold clarification:** Scaffold edits follow the same graph-output and conditional-diff rule as other projection edits (ADR-064).

### Consequences

- Do not use the earlier future-input-only interpretation as the expected behavior. Tests must check the new output graph after a projection edit and assert a diff only if the graph changes, as specified by ADR-064.
- This decision does not establish whether an explicit rebuild operation exists or how configuration versions, queued inputs, timers or stacked downstream projections are handled.

### Open questions

- At which precise input boundary does a configuration change take effect?
- Projection configuration is changed through a separate interface (ADR-046); its internal representation and any configuration events remain open.
- Can an explicit rebuild or replay be requested, and what does it emit?
- How are changes to an upstream projection's configuration observed by downstream projections?

title: Change projection configuration through a separate interface
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Input processing and projection edits can both lead to output graphs; a projection edit produces a new output graph which may or may not differ (ADR-064).

### Decision

Projection configuration changes reach the engine through a separate interface rather than the input event-ingestion interface.

### Consequences

- A verification schedule needs to represent configuration changes separately from ingested source events, even if both are steps in one test.
- Tests must synchronize configuration updates with subsequent input processing once the update's activation boundary is defined.
- This decision does not specify whether the separate interface is an API, editor, file loader, or combination, nor how it represents the configuration graph internally.
- It also does not determine whether the engine emits separate configuration-change events or stores configuration versions.

### Open questions

- What interface operations and formats create, edit, activate and remove projection configurations?
- How does an update interleave with previously accepted but unprocessed inputs?
- Is configuration state versioned, and what version is used by a deterministic replay?
- What processing barrier confirms that an update is active for future inputs?

title: Support input and logical-time test checkpoints
body:
**Status:** Accepted for verification harness  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The harness evaluates projection graphs and diffs at selected points. Tests may need to inspect state after a specified amount of input has been processed or at a meaningful logical time.

### Decision

Support both checkpoints after specified inputs and checkpoints at specified logical times.

### Consequences

- A test description can request checks after a specific event, batch or input count, and can request checks at logical timestamps.
- The harness must distinguish the logical time requested from proof that the relevant projection has processed the required inputs; a precise synchronization contract remains to be defined.
- Checkpoints can be applied to multiple projections and graph/diff expectations under their configured behavior, but cross-projection barriers and time controls are not yet specified.
- This decision does not mandate historical graph storage or define how the engine's clock is controlled.

### Open questions

- How does the harness advance or simulate logical time?
- How does it know that a given projection has fully processed an input or reached the requested checkpoint?
- What does a time checkpoint mean when late data can arrive after that time?
- Can a checkpoint require multiple projections or input streams to have reached a coordinated boundary?

title: Time passing alone does not change a projection graph
body:
**Status:** Clarified by ADR-064  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The harness can use logical-time checkpoints (ADR-047). The user was asked whether time passing alone can change a projection's graph. The earlier conclusion that only input processing can ever change the graph was too broad; projection edits also produce new output graphs (ADR-064).

### Decision

The passage of time by itself does not change the projection graph. Projection edits also produce new output graphs, which may differ (ADR-064).

### Consequences

- A test should advance the logical clock without delivering input and assert that the projection graph is unchanged and no graph diff is produced for the passage of time alone.
- A later input can still be interpreted using time-dependent information or policies; exactly how time is used remains open.
- Inputs can include graph and graph-diff inputs as well as other inputs (ADR-030). This decision does not limit input to raw telemetry.
- Do not assume an autonomous passage of time alone changes the graph. The exact mechanisms for expiry and stale-state transitions remain open.
- This decision does not address changes to the separate telemetry stream or lifecycle operations such as explicit projection deletion.

### Open questions

- Can a timer or explicit clock event be delivered as a projection input?
- Can a later ordinary input cause previously retained graph data to expire?
- What logical time and event-time information can projection rules access?
- What checkpoint barrier proves that no graph input was processed during a time-advance test?

title: Give entities an ontology type, including NoType
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

The user was asked whether every graph entity requires a type such as service, host or incident. The user answered: “Yes, NoType is also a type,” and clarified that types are part of the ontology.

### Decision

Entities have a type, and NoType is itself a type for an entity whose specific type is not otherwise known. Types are part of the ontology.

### Consequences

- Verification fixtures can represent a discovered entity as NoType rather than requiring the engine to invent a more specific classification.
- Tests should distinguish NoType from absent or invalid type according to the eventual input and output schema; exact validation behavior is not yet defined.
- Ontology design and mapping remain out of scope for the current work, but the graph contract must account for entity types belonging to the ontology.
- This decision does not specify the ontology's structure, type identifiers, inheritance, type updates, relationship typing or tenant-sharing rules.

### Open questions

- A NoType entity can be updated to a more specific type while keeping its identity; see ADR-050.
- Can an entity have multiple types?
- Relationship types are also defined by the tenant's ontology; see ADR-056.
- How are type versions and identifiers represented in portable tests?

title: Update an entity's type without replacing its identity
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Entities have ontology-backed types, including NoType when a more specific type is not known (ADR-049). Later input can provide better classification evidence.

### Decision

If an entity starts as NoType and later input identifies it as a service, update the existing entity's type while keeping its identity and produce a graph diff.

### Consequences

- Verification must check that the entity ID remains unchanged, its type changes, and the applicable projection's graph diff represents the update.
- The qualifying input changes graph data and thus is eligible for recent graph-affecting input history under the applicable retention contract.
- Existing relationships that refer to the same entity identity should not be assumed to require replacement solely due to the type update; exact relationship behavior needs specification.
- This specific example does not decide whether all type changes are allowed, how conflicts are resolved, or whether updates propagate automatically across projections.

### Open questions

- The same entity ID can have different types in different projections; see ADR-051.
- How are conflicting later classifications handled?
- Can a type be changed back to NoType or replaced by another specific type?

title: Allow projection-specific entity types
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

An underlying entity ID is shared across projections (ADR-001). Entities have ontology-backed types including NoType (ADR-049), and an entity's type can be updated as evidence arrives (ADR-050).

### Decision

The same entity ID can have different types in different projections. For example, one projection may classify it as NoType while another classifies it as Service.

### Consequences

- Entity identity and projection-specific classification must be tested independently; identical IDs do not imply identical types in all views.
- Test fixtures should show two projections containing the same ID with different types, then verify each projection's graph and diff behavior under its own rules.
- A type change in one projection is not assumed to automatically change another projection; propagation depends on their configured inputs and composition.
- The decision does not determine how conflicts are shown, whether an ontology can impose constraints across views, or how classification is stored internally.

### Open questions

- How are type changes propagated through stacked projections when the downstream projection consumes the upstream diff?
- Can one projection assign several ontology types to the same entity?
- How are conflicting classifications resolved when a projection consumes multiple graphs?

title: Use directional relationships
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Relationships have projection-specific identities (ADR-003) and are edges whose endpoints are entities, not other relationships (ADR-083). Their directionality is part of the graph contract.

### Decision

Relationships are always directional: each has a defined source and target.

### Consequences

- Tests must compare source and target, not merely whether two elements are connected.
- Reversing a relationship is a meaningful semantic difference; tests should include a direction-reversal negative case.
- A relationship cannot itself be an endpoint of another relationship (ADR-083).
- The decision does not specify relationship type constraints, identity keys, endpoint deletion behavior, self-links or how an unknown direction is represented.

### Open questions

- How should inputs with insufficient evidence to determine direction be represented or rejected?
- Are self-referential relationships allowed?
- Can multiple directed relationships of the same type connect the same endpoints?
- Are inverse relationships separate graph elements or derived views?

title: Allow relationships in both directions
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Relationships are directional (ADR-052). The user clarified that a relationship can also exist vice versa.

### Decision

The graph can contain a relationship from A to B and a relationship from B to A at the same time. Each direction is represented by a directional relationship.

### Consequences

- Verification must allow both directed relationships to coexist and distinguish their sources and targets.
- The existence of A → B alone does not establish that B → A also exists; test expectations must specify evidence or rules for each direction.
- This decision does not establish whether the two relationships share a type, are automatically created together, or have a special inverse association.

### Open questions

- Can each direction have a distinct relationship type and independent graph data?
- How are opposite-direction relationships identified and updated within a projection?
- Are reverse relationships inferred automatically under any configured rules?

title: Allow multiple same-direction relationships
body:
**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-11-07

### Context

Relationships are directed (ADR-052) and both directions may coexist (ADR-053). The same pair of entities may interact in more than one way.

### Decision

A projection can contain more than one relationship in the same direction between the same two entities.

### Consequences

- The harness must not identify a relationship solely by its source and target; tests need to represent distinct projection-specific relationship identities.
- Fixtures should include two relationships with the same directed endpoints and verify that their data and diffs are independently represented.
- This decision does not establish whether same-type relationships can share endpoints, what identity keys distinguish them, or whether relationship type is mandatory.

### Open questions

- Two relationships with the same source, target and type cannot coexist in one projection; see ADR-055.
- What makes two relationship observations refer to the same relationship rather than separate ones?
